clue.text: Denied scorer runs; had second thoughts

indicators.note: colours or dyes that run spread out of place, so the letters bleed into a new order

blocks.note: the twelve letters taken as written

explanation.surface: A striker is refused a goal after the runs are disallowed, and the officials change their minds.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Runs' reads like a cricket score attached to the scorer, but it is the signal to rearrange the two words before it.
explanation.definitionFit: To reconsider is to think again about a decision, which is exactly having second thoughts.

clue.text: Family member's heading off: joy!

indicators.note: when the heading goes off, the front letter of the word is removed

blocks.note: a relation is a member of one's family

explanation.surface: A relative sets off on a trip and someone is overjoyed to see them go.
explanation.walkthrough: The 's stands for 'is': the family member is having its heading taken off, losing its first letter R.
explanation.definitionFit: Elation is a feeling of great happiness and high spirits, a close synonym of joy.

clue.text: Oops – silly amounts of marsupials

indicators.note: something silly is muddled and nonsensical, so these letters lose their sensible order

blocks.note: taken as written
sums are amounts of money or quantities

explanation.surface: Someone apologises for miscounting the creatures, getting silly totals.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Silly amounts' looks like one phrase, but 'silly' works only on the exclamation before it, and 'amounts' stands alone.
explanation.definitionFit: Opossums are American pouched mammals, the best-known marsupials outside Australia.

clue.text: Help me, duck, OK?

blocks.note: SOS is the distress signal, a call for help
a duck is a score of nothing in cricket, which looks like the letter O

explanation.surface: A plea for assistance addressed affectionately to someone called 'duck', asking if they are all right.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Duck' is a British term of endearment in the surface; in cricket a duck is a score of zero, hence O.
explanation.definitionFit: Something so-so is merely passable, neither good nor bad, which is what lukewarm OK means.

clue.text: Wee drink at first satisfied (but only at first) theatrical types

indicators.note: keeping only what comes at first means taking just the opening letter of the preceding word

blocks.note: a dram is a small measure of spirits, especially whisky
taken as written
1st written with I for the digit one
the opening letter of the word

explanation.surface: Actors have a small whisky and are content, at least for a while.
explanation.walkthrough: 'First' is used twice: once as 1ST, read as IST, and once inside the parenthesis telling you to keep just the first letter of 'satisfied'.
explanation.definitionFit: Dramatists write plays, so they are people of the theatre, loosely called theatrical types.

clue.text: Religious leader's cut short talk

indicators.note: cutting something short trims off its end, so the final letter goes

blocks.note: in British slang to rabbit (on) is to talk at length

explanation.surface: A preacher's sermon was curtailed.
explanation.walkthrough: To rabbit, from rhyming slang 'rabbit and pork' for talk, means to chatter; lose its last letter T. The 's is 'is'.
explanation.definitionFit: A rabbi is the ordained teacher and spiritual head of a Jewish congregation.

clue.text: Gave 'old-fashioned' to describe Old Norse

indicators.note: to describe a shape is to draw around it, so one piece encircles another

blocks.note: dated means out of fashion
ON is the standard abbreviation for Old Norse

explanation.surface: Someone called the Old Norse language old-fashioned.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Describe' here has its geometric sense of tracing round something, not its sense of characterising.
explanation.definitionFit: To donate is to give something, typically to a charity or cause, so donated equals gave.

clue.text: A little Triple sec mixed with purée, zest — making ...?

definitions.text: A little Triple sec mixed with purée, zest — making ...?

indicators.note: a little of a word is a small part of it, here just its opening letter
ingredients that are mixed are stirred together, so these letters are jumbled

blocks.note: the opening letter of the word
taken as written
taken as written, accent dropped
taken as written

explanation.surface: A recipe: a dash of orange liqueur combined with purée and citrus zest makes a well-known dessert.
explanation.walkthrough: Triple sec is an orange liqueur, and orange zest and liqueur flavour the sauce, so the whole clue describes the dish as well as spelling it.
explanation.definitionFit: Crêpes Suzette are thin pancakes served in a caramelised orange and liqueur sauce, often flambéed.

clue.text: Fancifully, to date E.U. élite, you'll need perfume

indicators.note: something done fancifully is imaginative and free, so the letters are rearranged at will

blocks.note: the letters taken as written, ignoring dots and accent

explanation.surface: Advice that anyone hoping to court a European Union bigwig had better wear scent.
explanation.walkthrough: The dots in E.U. and the accent on élite are ignored; only the letters count.
explanation.definitionFit: Eau de toilette is a lightly concentrated scented water, a weaker form of fragrance worn on the skin.

clue.text: Reckons there's no time for mutiny, son

indicators.note: if there is no time in a word, the letter standing for time is dropped from it

blocks.note: mutiny is a form of treason against authority
S is the abbreviation for son

explanation.surface: Someone concludes that there is no time left for a rebellion by their boy.
explanation.walkthrough: T is the usual abbreviation for time, removed from the front of the word for mutiny.
explanation.definitionFit: To reason that something is so is to work it out and conclude, as someone who reckons does.

clue.text: Country's 'Bravo' welcomed by Shearer, international ace

indicators.note: a guest who is welcomed is taken inside, so one piece sits within another

blocks.note: Bravo is B in the NATO phonetic alphabet
Alan Shearer is the former England football captain
I is a standard abbreviation for international
A is the abbreviation for ace on playing cards

explanation.surface: A nation applauds its star footballer as he plays in an international match.
explanation.walkthrough: Alan Shearer is a famous English centre forward; 'international ace' looks like a description of him but splits into two single letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Albania is a Balkan nation on the Adriatic coast, its capital Tirana.

clue.text: We're told trim's wanting braces

indicators.note: what we are told reaches us through the ears, so it is the sound that counts

blocks.note: trims means cuts back, which is pares

explanation.surface: Apparently someone's slim figure needs support from braces on their trousers.
explanation.walkthrough: A brace is a pair, especially of game birds, so braces are pairs; British braces are also what Americans call suspenders, which the surface leans on.
explanation.definitionFit: Brace as a noun means two of a kind, as in a brace of pheasants, so braces are couples of things.

clue.text: I sat first, dined on date, and filled up

blocks.note: the word sat placed before I
to dine is to eat a meal
D is the abbreviation for date, placed on the end

explanation.surface: A diner describes taking their seat first, eating on a date, and feeling full.
explanation.walkthrough: 'I sat first' tells you to put SAT before I; 'on' then adds the date's abbreviation after the meal.
explanation.definitionFit: Satiated means having eaten or had enough to be completely satisfied, as when one is full.

clue.text: Inept Clanger lying down

blocks.note: a clanger is a blatant blunder
prone means lying face down

explanation.surface: A bungler's gaffe leaves them flat on the floor.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Clanger' is British slang for an embarrassing mistake, from the sound of dropping something; the capital letter tries to suggest a proper noun.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone error-prone keeps making mistakes, so they are clumsy or incompetent, which is inept.

clue.text: Polish damage metal flyer

blocks.note: to sand is to smooth by rubbing
to mar is to spoil
tin is a metallic element

explanation.surface: Something from Poland harms a metal aircraft.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Polish' is capitalised as the first word, tempting a reading about Poland; it is the verb meaning to smooth.
explanation.definitionFit: The sand martin is a small brown swallow-like bird that nests in sandy banks, so a bird that flies.

clue.text: Modify part of expedition

indicators.note: a part of a word is a run of its letters, so the answer sits inside it

blocks.note: letters two to five of the word

explanation.surface: Someone changes one stage of a trip.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer lies inside the last word, running from its third letter.
explanation.definitionFit: To edit a text or plan is to change or revise it, the same as altering it.

clue.text: Primarily, a loyal shepherd's assistant: trustworthy intelligent animal named ...?

definitions.text: Primarily, a loyal shepherd's assistant: trustworthy intelligent animal named ...?

indicators.note: primarily means first of all, so only the leading letters are kept

blocks.clueFragment: a loyal shepherd's assistant: trustworthy intelligent animal named
blocks.note: the opening letter of each of the eight words

explanation.surface: A description of a faithful, clever working dog that helps a shepherd, ending by asking its name.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue both spells the answer through its initial letters and describes it: the breed is also called the German shepherd dog.
explanation.definitionFit: The Alsatian is the British name for the German shepherd, a loyal and intelligent working dog breed.

clue.text: Bone found in Dublin Bay oddly ignored

indicators.note: ignoring the odd-numbered positions leaves only the even ones

blocks.note: the second, fourth, sixth and eighth letters

explanation.surface: A skeleton is discovered in an Irish bay, and strangely nobody pays attention.
explanation.walkthrough: Drop the first, third, fifth, seventh and ninth letters of the place name and the even ones remain.
explanation.definitionFit: The ulna is the longer of the two bones of the human forearm, on the little-finger side.

clue.text: After a month, Fitzgerald's written shortish book

blocks.note: Nov is the calendar abbreviation for November
Ella Fitzgerald, the American jazz singer

explanation.surface: A month later, the author Fitzgerald has produced a short work.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface points to F. Scott Fitzgerald the novelist; the wordplay wants the jazz singer Ella, placed after the month.
explanation.definitionFit: A novella is a work of prose fiction longer than a short story but shorter than a full novel.

clue.text: Little iron supply in pasta

indicators.note: read as supple-ly, flexibly, so the letters bend into a new shape

blocks.note: the letters taken as written

explanation.surface: Pasta contains only a small amount of the mineral iron.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Supply' looks like a noun meaning provision, but read as the adverb from supple, flexibly, it signals the rearrangement.
explanation.definitionFit: Tortellini are small ring-shaped stuffed Italian dumplings, one of many kinds of pasta.

clue.text: Jerome K Jerome's central character?

blocks.note: surface reading: the protagonist of a book by the author of Three Men in a Boat
setter's reading: the letter in the middle of his name, the K standing for Klapka

explanation.walkthrough: 'Character' means a letter, not a person in a story: the K sitting in the middle of the author's name stands for his middle name.
explanation.definitionFit: A middle letter standing for a name, like the K in his name, is what we call a person's first letter abbreviation.

clue.text: Retreating in South Pole, five numb Englishmen initially wanting blankets

indicators.note: initially means at the start, so only the first letters are taken
retreating means going backwards, so the assembled string runs the other way

blocks.note: S is the compass abbreviation
taken as written
V is the Roman numeral for five
the opening letter of the word
the opening letter of the word

explanation.surface: Polar explorers in retreat, frozen and numb, desperately need blankets.
explanation.walkthrough: The scene evokes Scott's expedition; the pieces are strung together and then read backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: To envelop is to wrap or cover completely, so envelops means covers like a blanket, used as a verb.

clue.text: Actor, not quietly, portraying chicken?

indicators.note: not having something means it is left out, so a letter is removed

blocks.note: a player is a stage performer
p, piano, is the musical direction for quietly

explanation.surface: A performer loudly playing the part of a chicken.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags that the definition is by example: a laying hen is one kind of chicken.
explanation.definitionFit: A layer is a hen kept for laying eggs, so a chicken is one example of the word.

clue.text: Part of record that might be whispered

blocks.note: first meaning: the main side of a single, carrying the lead track
second meaning: a remark spoken so others nearby do not hear, as on stage

explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests a hushed section of a recording; the hyphenated record side and the theatrical remark are separate meanings.
explanation.definitionFit: An actor's aside is a muttered comment for the audience alone, while a single's A-side is its principal track.

clue.text: Tippling eggnog to begin with, Everyman returned to chuck it down

indicators.note: what comes to begin with is at the start, so only opening letters are kept
something returned comes back the way it went, so it is written backwards

blocks.note: the opening letter of the word
the opening letter of the word
the setter refers to himself, so his name stands for me

explanation.surface: The setter, after drinking eggnog, came home and threw it up.
explanation.walkthrough: Setters often use their own pseudonym for ME. 'Chuck it down' is British slang for rain heavily.
explanation.definitionFit: To teem is to pour with rain, and to chuck it down is an informal idiom for a heavy downpour.

clue.text: Count up, then: 'House!' (a bloodthirsty call)

blocks.note: to tally is to add up a total
HO is an abbreviation for house

explanation.surface: A bingo caller counts the numbers and someone shouts 'House!' with alarming enthusiasm.
explanation.walkthrough: 'House!' is the shout of a winning bingo player, which colours the surface; HO is simply its abbreviation.
explanation.definitionFit: Tally-ho is the cry of fox hunters on sighting the quarry, so a call urging on the kill.

clue.text: The French retorted: 'It is time to be snobby'

indicators.note: a retort turns words back, so the piece is read in the opposite direction

blocks.note: le is French for 'the'
taken as written
T is the abbreviation for time

explanation.surface: A Frenchman snaps back that the moment has come for some snobbery.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Retorted' sounds like speech, but here it means turned back, reversing the French article.
explanation.definitionFit: An elitist attitude favours a privileged few and looks down on others, which is being snobbish.

clue.text: Marines trial exercises in transport hubs

indicators.note: exercising works and moves things about, so these letters are put through new positions

blocks.note: the letters taken as written

explanation.surface: Military forces test their drills at airports and stations.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Exercises' looks like the marines' training, but it is the instruction to rearrange the two words.
explanation.definitionFit: Air terminals are airport buildings where passengers board flights, central points of travel networks.
